Winslow Tandler ← Issue 11
SECOND ORDER
Issue 12 · September 14, 2026
AI, Capital & Work

Data Centers: The Host's Terms

The objections to data centers, tested against the primary records, and the local rule behind each outcome.

Read the companion deck (PDF)→

SUMMARY

Gallup found in 2026 that 71 percent of Americans would oppose an AI data center in their area, and by August towns in 42 states had adopted or proposed more than 500 local moratoria. The complaints are much the same everywhere, that a campus uses too much water, raises power bills, adds carbon, makes noise and hires almost no one. Those are fair concerns, and the places that have hosted data centers longest have a record that answers them. This issue takes the complaints one at a time, as a series of case studies.

A campus brings a town new demand for electricity, water, housing and workers, and nearly every complaint is about that demand. It also brings a large block of taxable property, and since a finished campus employs few people, the property tax is where most of the town's gain comes from. Whether residents come out ahead depends on whether power, housing and workers keep up with the new demand, and on how much of the tax the town keeps. Towns, counties and states decide both through tax rates, abatements, permits and grid rules.

Each section can be read with the same two questions in mind, whether supply kept up with the new demand and who collected the tax. Where the rules let supply and revenue keep pace, residents came out ahead, as homeowners in Quincy, Washington, and Loudoun County, Virginia, did through lower property tax rates. Where supply came late, as with housing in Abilene, Texas, and power plants in Virginia, renters and ratepayers paid more. The same rules shape emissions, since nearly all of a campus's carbon comes from the plants built to serve it. Two sections check widely repeated figures, the fall in Quincy's poverty rate and a water comparison from Chile.

The costs we found fall mostly on renters and on the households nearest a campus. Costs that narrow can explain opposition next door and are hard to square with opposition from seven in ten Americans. A moratorium avoids those costs, and it also gives up the tax and the chance to set the terms that decided the outcome in the places we studied.

Source names in blue link to the release, paper or dashboard the figure is taken from.

01 · EVIDENCE

The claim of little local return

The usual complaint is that a data center gives little back to its town because it hires so few people. Its biggest payment to the town is the property tax, and Quincy, Washington, which has had data centers since 2007, has the longest record of what that tax did to other owners' rates.

Every property owner in Quincy pays a share of what the city, the school district, the hospital district, the county and a handful of smaller districts levy. Washington limits each of those districts to 1 percent more than the year before, plus whatever new construction adds. So when the value of existing property jumps, a district can't collect the windfall and has to lower the rate instead. The same cap applies in two nearby cities, Ephrata, the county seat, and Moses Lake, the county's largest city. All three buy the same cheap hydropower from Grant County PUD, though Moses Lake has a few data centers of its own, so the comparison doesn't isolate the data centers completely.

In the Department of Revenue's levy files, Quincy's taxable value goes from $265 million in 2005 to $6.1 billion in 2025, 23 times as much, or about fourteen times after inflation (Exhibit 1). Over the same years Ephrata's value roughly tripled and Moses Lake's grew almost fivefold. Quincy's city levy rate fell 70 percent, from $3.10 per thousand dollars of value to $0.92. Ephrata's fell 42 percent and Moses Lake's 17 percent, under the same cap. Quincy still collected far more money, $5.6 million in 2025 against $820,000 in 2005, because the cap lets a district collect extra on new construction, and much of what got built in Quincy was data centers. The city's rate fell furthest of the three because its tax base grew fastest.

A homeowner's actual bill adds up the rates of every district that covers the house, schools and hospital included. In Quincy that combined rate was $8.17 per $1,000 of value in 2026, down from about $14.81 in 2005, a drop of about 45 percent. That happened even though voters approved bonds for a new high school and a new hospital along the way. On a home assessed at $300,000, the 2005 rate would come to $4,443 a year. The 2026 rate comes to $2,451.

The data center buildings also add to the school district's tax base without adding pupils. The companies came to Quincy for Grant County PUD's cheap hydropower, which few towns can offer.

Washington's 2010 sales tax exemption for data center servers applies only in rural counties like Grant, and the state's auditors found in 2016 that most of the companies claiming it were in Quincy. Grant County PUD charges big new customers at least the market price of power and makes them pay for the generation and transmission built to serve them, so other customers don't carry those costs. Its eight data center operators used 37 percent of the county's power in 2025.

02 · EVIDENCE

The poverty series

Supporters of the campuses point to Quincy's poverty rate, which fell from about 29 percent to about 6 percent. If the data centers caused that, it would matter more to residents than the lower tax rate. The Census Bureau's five-year estimates put Quincy's poverty rate at 29.4 percent for 2008 to 2012 and somewhere between 6 and 13 percent in the two most recent releases. The drop is large on either release (Exhibit 2).

The starting window, 2008 to 2012, includes the recession and begins a year after the first campus opened, so comparing it with 2020 to 2024 isn't a clean before-and-after test.

The Department of Revenue's workgroup counted about 900 direct data center jobs in Quincy, which is still mostly a farm and food-processing town, and nobody has published a count of how many of those workers live there. Nadia Bucio, who owns a restaurant in town, told the Spokesman-Review in July 2026, "I don't think it's just been the data centers." Brookings' May 2026 study of host counties across the country found data-processing employment up and wages unchanged. The census numbers record a big drop in poverty, and no one has measured how much of it the campuses caused.

03 · EVIDENCE

The tax contribution and the tax break

Loudoun County, Virginia, also lowered homeowners' rates, though no state rule required it. The supervisors chose to tax data center equipment at the county's full rate and used the money to cut the real estate rate.

Loudoun calls its cluster of data centers the largest in the world, and with that many campuses taxed at the full rate, its receipts are about the most a host can collect. The county taxes the computers inside a data center as personal property at $4.15 per $100 of value. For fiscal 2027 the supervisors budgeted $879 million from data center equipment and another $418 million in real property tax on the same buildings. Together that's about two of every five dollars in the general fund (Exhibit 3). As the equipment tax grew, Loudoun cut its real estate rate from $1.205 per $100 in tax year 2013 to $0.805 in tax year 2025, and left it there for 2026.

Lower rates haven't stopped bills from rising, because assessments keep going up. The supervisors expect the average existing homeowner's bill to rise from $6,280 to $6,427 in fiscal 2027. At the 2013 rate of $1.205, that same bill would be about $9,600.

The equipment tax alone pays for about 27 percent of Loudoun's general fund, and computers lose taxable value as they age, so the money depends on operators replacing them. In January 2026 Loudoun's budget staff wrote that operators were holding on to equipment longer than the five years the county's models assumed. The staff proposed putting surplus revenue into one-time capital projects, so that the county's ongoing spending doesn't come to depend on the equipment tax.

Virginia law (section 58.1-3506) lets each county set its own rate on data center equipment, up to its general rate, and the six counties we compared charge anywhere from $0.66 to $4.57 per $100 today (Exhibit 4). Prince William raised its rate four budgets in a row, to $4.50 for 2026. That's as high as state law lets it go, because a county can't tax data center equipment above its general personal property rate, and Prince William's general rate is $4.50 while Fairfax's is $4.57. Henrico cut its rate in 2017 to $0.40, about a tenth of Loudoun's, to attract data centers, then raised it to $2.60 for 2025. Even at $0.40, Henrico collected enough from data centers to seed a $60 million housing trust fund in 2024.

The state, meanwhile, gives up sales tax on the same equipment. Virginia puts the cost at $928.6 million for fiscal 2023, counting state, local and regional shares. An industry-commissioned study for the Northern Virginia Technology Council put the industry's Virginia tax payments for 2022 at $1 billion local and $640 million state. The two estimates cover different years and use different accounting, so they can't be netted against each other.

The industry says the exemption is why the equipment is in Virginia at all. Critics say most of it would have been installed anyway, with the tax paid. Neither side has put a number on how much investment the exemption brought in or what that investment returned after public costs. In 2026 the legislature kept the exemption and added a two-year tax of 1.1 cents per kilowatt-hour on data center electricity, with up to $600 million a year going to the general fund.

04 · EVIDENCE

Few permanent jobs and temporary work

A finished campus employs few people, about fifty in a building the size of four football fields, which is also why it adds so little to what a county spends on schools and services. For a host town, the bigger effect of the industry's jobs comes during construction, when a crew in the thousands pushes up local rents and wages for several years.

Virginia's Joint Legislative Audit and Review Commission (JLARC) counted about fifty full-time workers in a typical 250,000 square foot data center, or one per 5,000 square feet. A distribution center that size employs almost eight times as many. The fifty earned about $100,000 on average in 2024. Microsoft says it pays its Central Washington data center staff an average of $93,000, about 75 percent more than the regional average of $53,000 (Exhibit 5). None of the sources we looked at records where those workers live.

In JLARC's model of the industry's yearly impact on Virginia, construction accounts for 80 percent of the jobs and the labor income, about 59,000 of 74,000 jobs, and those jobs end when the building is finished. A campus takes five years or more to build out, and operators told JLARC that about 1,500 workers are on site at the busiest point of building a single facility. At the much bigger Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas, Oracle reported 9,000 construction jobs in the summer of 2026, against 1,000 long-term jobs once it's done. That crew was about a tenth of the Abilene area's entire labor force of 89,743 in July 2026, and all of those people needed somewhere to live and were hired away from other employers. Higher rents and higher wages for local builders are the costs a host town has to set against the campus's tax.

Skillit's figures, reported by Fortune in December 2025, put the average data center construction worker at $81,800 a year, against $62,000 on other projects, a 32 percent premium, and the crews spend that money locally while the work lasts. They also need somewhere to live, and KUT, the public radio station in Austin, found Abilene's average listed rent up nearly 50 percent in a year, to about $2,600 a month, while the Texas average fell about 1 percent. Zillow's rent index for the Abilene area rose 37 percent over the year to July 2026, from $1,460 to $2,003 a month. KUT also reported that the local housing shelter's time to place someone had gone from just over a month to as long as six. Rents slipped 0.3 percent between June and July 2026 on Zillow's index, which is too little to say whether they've peaked.

Whether a host is paid for those costs depends on the tax terms it sets. Loudoun taxes data center equipment at the full rate and used the money to cut the real estate rate for everyone else. Abilene's council chose to abate 85 percent of the campus's property tax, which means the city collects a fraction of the tax while its renters pay the higher rents. On Oracle's estimate, the 15 percent the council kept is worth about $30 million a year, so the city is giving up about $170 million a year.

The council approved the abatement on February 13, 2025, for ten years, the longest Texas allows. The agreement sets minimums for jobs, for the average wage ($57,600) and for taxable value ($200 million a building), and it contains nothing about housing. Under its abatement policy, Abilene asks applicants to describe a project's effect on the local housing market but attaches no condition to the answer. The council dealt with housing afterward, through zoning, and by January 2026 had approved a 957-space RV park for data center workers. On the Census Bureau's permit counts, builders were authorized to build 527 housing units in the Abilene metropolitan area in 2024, 1,160 in 2025 and 1,363 in the first seven months of 2026 (Exhibit 6). The 2026 count includes 529 apartments, after none in the two years before. Builders responded within about a year, but none of those apartments will be occupied before 2027, and renters are paying the higher rents in the meantime.

Gene Lantrip, an Abilene homebuilder, told the Texas Tribune in April 2026 that he'd lost two lead electricians and their helpers to the data centers and that his houses now take two months longer to build. Scotty Wristen of WE Electric lost five electricians. The Tribune reported that a homebuilder's electrician in Texas earns $20 an hour, while a data center offers $35, 75 percent more before overtime and per diem. Bloomberg reported that advertised pay for commercial electricians on Indeed rose 9.9 percent in the year to May 2026, about four times the 2.4 percent rise across all advertised jobs, and Deloitte reports that utilities are competing with data centers for the same electricians. A homebuilder who wants to keep his electricians has to pay something closer to the data center rate, and the higher wages and the slower builds both end up in the price of the house. JLARC's construction figures count the crew's income, but they don't count the higher rents and wages that the host town's renters and other employers pay, so they overstate the benefit to any single town.

05 · EVIDENCE

The Cerrillos figure

In Empire of AI, published in May 2025, Karen Hao wrote that a Google data center proposed for Cerrillos, Chile, could use more than a thousand times the water of the town's roughly eighty-eight thousand residents. The numbers in the Chilean filing behind that sentence were labeled "litros de agua," liters of water, but they were actually cubic meters, so her ratio was a thousand times too high. Andy Masley caught the error in November 2025, and on December 17 Hao published a correction, calling the comparison "off by a factor of 1,000." The corrected passage says the campus "could use more water than the entire population of Cerrillos," which works out to about one to one. We check the corrected figure against the operators' own numbers in section 06.

06 · EVIDENCE

The question of water

Critics also say a data center uses more water than the people around it. The widely repeated claim that a 20 megawatt cluster is filled once with 20,000 gallons has no public source, so we worked from the operators' own cooling figures. An evaporative campus can use more than two hundred times the water of a closed-loop campus of the same size, and a town can look at the design before it approves the project.

Microsoft reported a fleet average of 0.30 liters per kilowatt-hour for fiscal 2024. At that rate, a 20 megawatt IT load running around the clock uses about 14 million gallons a year, roughly what 460 Americans use at home (Exhibit 7). Since August 2024 Microsoft has specified a closed-loop design for every new site, meant to use no water for cooling, and Oracle and Vantage have published similar designs. Vantage expects its Port Washington campus to use at most 22,000 gallons a day, compared with 5 million for an evaporative campus of the same size, less than 1 percent as much. Virginia's auditors found that all of the state's data centers together account for less than 0.5 percent of state water withdrawals. In Quincy the data centers take 4 to 8 percent of the city's water, and the food processors take more than half.

The power plants that feed a campus use more water than the campus does. For the same 20 megawatt cluster, those plants consume about 65 million gallons a year on the Geological Survey's 2015 figures, and about 250 million on Lawrence Berkeley's figures, which count evaporation from hydro reservoirs. That's roughly five to eighteen times the campus's own 14 million gallons. Power plants use that water no matter what the electricity is for, so we count it as part of the grid's water use, which every customer shares.

The campuses that have taken a big share of a town's water are the ones with evaporative cooling towers. Google's three sites in The Dalles, Oregon, used 355 million gallons in 2021, 29 percent of the city's consumption, and about a third by 2024, according to OPB's reporting of city records.

The Dalles council voted unanimously in 2021 to let Google take over water rights from a closed aluminum smelter, along with $28.5 million of Google-funded wells, reservoirs and a pump station. When The Oregonian asked how much city water Google had used in 2021, the city sued the newspaper, arguing that the amount was Google's trade secret. It later settled and released the figure in December 2022. Under Minnesota's 2025 law, the permitting agency has to consider closed-loop cooling for any data center that would use more than 100 million gallons a year. Chandler, Arizona, has required every large-meter user to file a water plan with its development application since 2015. Virginia's auditors asked the legislature in December 2024 to give localities clear authority to require a water estimate before a rezoning. And Loudoun Water built a reclaimed water system for data center cooling back in 2010. Under the Minnesota and Chandler rules and the Virginia proposal, the government knows a campus's expected water use, or at least its cooling design, before it approves one.

07 · EVIDENCE

The price of power

A data center pushes up household electricity prices when the power plants needed to serve it come late, and the rules that decide how fast a new plant gets connected differ between Texas and PJM, the grid that serves Virginia. Through 2024, two studies published in June 2026 found no rise in residential rates or household bills from data center growth. Watten, Bistline and Blanford estimate that from 2019 to 2024 the average residential customer's state had rates about 6 percent lower than it would have without data center growth, because utilities could spread their fixed costs over more kilowatt-hours. Kiran Garimella at Rutgers compared ZIP codes that got a data center between 2014 and 2024 with ZIP codes whose bills had looked similar, and found no statistically significant increase in household bills. Neither study reaches June 1, 2025, when the first high capacity price on the PJM grid took effect.

Virginia, the state critics bring up most, has had residential power prices below the national average every month since January 2010, on EIA's monthly figures (Exhibit 8). From 2019 to 2024 the Virginia price fell 2.7 percent after inflation while the national price rose 3.2 percent. Then, in the twelve months to June 2026, the Virginia price rose 11.6 percent against 6.6 percent nationally, on preliminary data.

The biggest new piece of that increase is the capacity charge, which utilities pay PJM to keep enough power plants on call for the hours of peak demand and then pass on to customers. No regulator has yet broken the increase down by cause. PJM's capacity price went from $28.92 per megawatt-day in the 2024/25 auction to $269.92 for 2025/26, more than nine times as much, and each of the three auctions since has cleared at the cap. Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor, assigns $29.4 billion of the last four auctions' $63.6 billion cost, almost half, to data center load. In November 2025 the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved base-rate increases of about 9 percent over 2026 and 2027 for a typical Dominion household. It also created a new class for customers of 25 megawatts or more, who have to pay for at least 85 percent of the transmission and distribution capacity they contract for, whether or not they use it. The commission set those terms so that other customers are covered if the big users end up using less than they said.

Kay, Reaser and Taylor at the Dallas Fed estimated in March 2026 that data center load raised wholesale power prices by about $5 a megawatt-hour in northern Virginia, more than 10 percent, and by less than $1 in Texas. They credit the Texas result to Texas building more new supply than any other region, or, in their words, "when supply is elastic, new load primarily increases production with modest price effects." Cleanview counts about 90 gigawatts of on-site generation announced by the industry and about 2 operating. The pledge by seven companies in March 2026 to pay "the full cost" of the generation they need covers plants that mostly haven't been built.

Texas can build that fast partly because ERCOT, its grid operator, makes connecting a plant simpler. ERCOT checks a new plant for reliability only, doesn't promise that its power can reach every corner of the system, and by its own account takes 18 to 30 months to connect a large plant. The generator doesn't pay for upgrades to the wider network either, which Lawrence Berkeley's researchers think is one reason more ERCOT projects make it to a signed agreement. In 2024, 14 gigawatts of new capacity started running in Texas. In PJM, nearly every project asks for network service, which means PJM first studies whether the plant's power can be delivered anywhere on the system, and that study takes longer. On Lawrence Berkeley's numbers, ERCOT requests reached an agreement in 24 months on average, against 41 months for network service elsewhere, and many PJM projects never sign at all. PJM says 74 percent of the projects it has studied since 2020 withdrew, and of the 103 gigawatts that did sign agreements, only 23, about one in five, are running. PJM's July 2026 auction for 2028/29 cleared at the cap and still came up about 6,800 megawatts short of what reliability requires.

Virginia's Clean Economy Act of 2020 requires Dominion to retire every carbon-emitting plant by 2045. On Dominion's count, 97 percent of the 234 gigawatts waiting in PJM's queue is solar, wind and storage, and 6.6 gigawatts is gas. Texas also has a big fleet of gas plants, and no study has yet separated how much of its small price effect comes from its connection rules and how much from its fuel.

Under Texas Senate Bill 6, signed in June 2025, a load of 75 megawatts or more has to contribute to the cost of connecting it, and a transmission-voltage load connected after 2025 has to let the grid cut its power in a shortage. Oregon and Minnesota told their utility commissions in 2025 to create a separate rate class for large loads, and Virginia's commission created one in November 2025. PJM opened a new queue cycle in April 2026 that promises answers in one to two years, and hasn't yet reached an agreement on that timeline.

In August 2026 Governor Abbott ordered the PUC and ERCOT to verify and audit every data center in the connection process before approving more. ERCOT was weighing about 474 gigawatts of requests to connect, about 90 percent of them data centers, more than five times its record peak demand. It paused its study of large loads and stopped approving new data centers of 75 megawatts or more to energize until the audit is done, with a report due to the PUC in December.

08 · EVIDENCE

Emissions, efficiency and nuclear power

Critics also say data centers are adding a lot of carbon to the air. Almost all of a campus's emissions come from the power plants that supply it, so how much carbon it adds depends on what the grid builds to serve it, and that's largely up to the state.

For now the total is modest. US data centers used 176 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2023, 4.4 percent of the country's total and about two thirds of what American homes used for air conditioning in 2020, on Lawrence Berkeley's and EIA's figures. Generating that power emitted about 61 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent, a little over 1 percent of US energy-related emissions, or about what 13 million cars emit in a year. A single query barely registers. Google puts its median Gemini text prompt at 0.24 watt-hours, and at the average grid's emission rate a typical car emits as much CO2 driving one mile as nearly 5,000 of those prompts. The concern is the growth, with Lawrence Berkeley projecting data centers at 6.7 to 12 percent of US electricity by 2028 and the IEA expecting them to account for nearly half of US demand growth through 2030.

With that much new demand coming, the plants built to meet it will set most of the future emissions, and we put a number on that choice in Exhibit 9. We took demand out to 2028 on Lawrence Berkeley's range and tried five ways of supplying the growth after 2025, from all carbon-free power to gas turbines with old coal plants kept open. With all carbon-free power, data center emissions would fall from about 89 million tons in 2025 to about 72 million in 2028, however much demand grew, because the rest of the grid keeps getting cleaner. With turbines and coal, the same growth would push them to about 230 million, more than three times as much and well above the 130 million tons that domestic airline flights emitted in 2022. On the average projection the choice of supply is worth about 160 million tons a year, while the gap between low and high demand, even with new gas plants, is about 100 million. The forecasts themselves disagree a lot. EPRI raised its forecast in February to 9 to 17 percent of US electricity by 2030, and Grid Strategies thinks utilities are overstating 2030 data center load by about 25 gigawatts, but in our numbers the supply matters more than which forecast turns out right.

Texas and Virginia, the two grids this issue keeps coming back to, are building different kinds of supply. Of the roughly 29,000 megawatts that started running on ERCOT's grid in 2024 and 2025, only about 3 percent was gas, by our count of EIA's generator data, and nearly all the rest was solar, batteries and wind. Dominion's 2025 plan for Virginia adds 8.5 gigawatts of new gas and retires none of its existing plants, coal included, and the company has told regulators it sees no viable path to closing all its carbon-emitting plants by 2045, as the state's Clean Economy Act requires. So a new campus in Texas is being met mostly with new solar and batteries, and one in Virginia with new gas and older plants kept running. Part of that difference goes back to the connection rules in section 07, which let Texas add plants faster.

The one source that can run a campus around the clock with almost no emissions is nuclear, and for decades licensing and building a reactor in the US has been slow. Over its life a reactor produces about 12 grams of CO2 per kilowatt-hour on the IPCC's estimates, against 490 for a gas plant, and US reactors ran 91 percent of the time in 2025, more than any other source. Even so, the only reactors the US has finished since 2016 are the two new units at Vogtle in Georgia.

Congress started loosening the licensing rules with the ADVANCE Act of 2024, which told the NRC that its licensing should not "unnecessarily limit" nuclear energy and cut its fees for advanced reactors by more than half. Executive orders in May 2025 set an 18-month deadline for licensing decisions and a goal of quadrupling US nuclear capacity to 400 gigawatts by 2050. In March 2026 the NRC approved construction of TerraPower's reactor in Wyoming, the first commercial construction approval in ten years, after a review of less than 18 months. Illinois and New Jersey lifted their bans on new reactors in 2026, and Texas has put $350 million into an advanced nuclear fund. Of the three closed US reactors being restarted, two have data center buyers, Microsoft at Three Mile Island and Google at Duane Arnold in Iowa, and Amazon and Meta have signed long contracts for the output of Susquehanna in Pennsylvania and Clinton in Illinois. The industry blamed for new emissions is paying to bring closed reactors back, in the places where the rules allow it.

All of these numbers assume demand grows the way the forecasts say, and it might not, because chips and models keep getting more efficient. Nvidia says its Blackwell Ultra systems turn out up to 50 times as many tokens per megawatt as the Hopper chips before them, and Google reports that the energy behind its median Gemini prompt fell 33-fold in the year to May 2025. Naveen Rao, who ran AI at Databricks, raised $475 million in December 2025 for Unconventional AI, which is aiming for chips 1,000 times more energy efficient than conventional ones are expected to be around 2030. Models are also shrinking to sizes phones and laptops can run. Stanford's AI Index found that the smallest model scoring above 60 percent on a standard knowledge test went from 540 billion parameters in 2022 to 3.8 billion in 2024. In a preprint, Jon Saad-Falcon and his co-authors found that small local models could handle 88.7 percent of chat and reasoning queries and cut energy use by 60 to 80 percent.

So far, though, cheaper computing has meant more computing, the pattern economists call the Jevons paradox. Google says it gets six times as much computing from each unit of electricity as it did five years ago, and its data centers still used 27 percent more electricity in 2024. The tokens Google processes each month went from about 480 trillion to more than 3.2 quadrillion in a year. Efficiency changes how much power AI uses, and in Exhibit 9 that moves emissions less than where the power comes from. A query answered on a phone still runs on power from the local grid.

Efficiency does raise a different risk for host towns, because if it pulls demand below the forecasts, some of the gas plants and power lines built for data centers will sit partly idle and someone has to pay for them. Whether that's the data centers or everyone else on the grid depends on terms the state's regulators set before the plants are built. Virginia's new class for the largest customers, from section 07, requires 14-year contracts and minimum payments of 60 percent of the generation they reserve and 85 percent of the transmission and distribution. AEP Ohio requires 85 percent for up to 12 years, and after its tariff took effect only about 13,000 of the 30,000 megawatts of data center requests in its territory paid for a study. Meta is paying for all three gas turbines Entergy is building for Hyperion, its campus in Richland Parish (section 10), on a 15-year contract. Under terms like these, if the load doesn't show up, the data center pays for most of what was built for it for the first 12 to 15 years, which the Louisiana Illuminator notes is about half the working life of a gas turbine.

09 · EVIDENCE

Noise and backup generators

People living near some Virginia campuses hear a low hum that the county noise rules weren't written to measure, and a county can only limit that sound if state law gives it the power to do so before the campus is built. Prince William County's consultant measured background noise at homes with no data center nearby at 43 decibels at night and 48 during the day, against residential limits of 55 and 60 (Exhibit 10). The consultant also confirmed what residents had been reporting, a 90 hertz tone likely to be audible indoors. The county's ordinance is written in A-weighted decibels, a scale that heavily discounts a tone that low, so a campus can comply with the ordinance and still be heard inside nearby homes.

In December 2024 Virginia's auditors found that data centers "emit low-frequency noise that is not loud enough to damage nearby residents' hearing and rarely loud enough to violate noise ordinances," and that most draw no complaints "because of their location or design." Some residents, the auditors added, say the constant sound affects their well-being. After $2 million of consultants' work, Prince William's supervisors set limits for industrial property of 73 decibels by day and 68 at night in October 2025, compared with 60 and 55 at homes.

JLARC found that Virginia localities didn't have clear authority to require a sound study before approving a campus, or to set a limit using a low-frequency measure, and recommended that the legislature give them both. Prince William's 2025 limits are in A-weighted decibels because that's the only scale the county's authority covers. Chandler, Arizona, has since January 2023 capped a campus's noise at the level measured before construction.

Virginia's auditors found the state's backup generators running 10 to 30 minutes a month for maintenance plus one annual test of one to four hours, or about three to ten scheduled hours a year, against the 100 hours federal rules allow for maintenance and testing (Exhibit 10). Actual emissions in 2023 were 7 percent of what the permits allowed, which fits with limited running. Some campuses have installed gas turbines while they wait for a grid connection, and xAI's turbines in Memphis were permitted in July 2025 to run continuously, after months of running without a permit.

10 · EVIDENCE

Opposition and what it establishes

Gallup found that 71 percent of Americans would oppose an AI data center in their own area, and Heatmap's tracking poll put support at 21 percent in May 2026, down from 43 percent in September 2025. Property owners across a town get a lower rate because of the campus's tax, while renters pay higher rents and the households closest to the campus hear the noise, so the people carrying the costs can reasonably oppose a campus that pays the town more than it costs. Counties report their receipts only as totals, so nobody can tell from them whether a particular household comes out ahead.

Most of the support at hearings comes from organized labor. In Westfield, Massachusetts, where a proposed campus would bring 1,800 construction jobs, the Boston Globe found the building trades were nearly the only group that turned out in favor, and the trades have told their locals to fight the moratoriums. National Nurses United supports the federal moratorium bill, and the flight attendants' president has called for a slowdown, though neither union has members working on a data center site.

Towns have also written that opposition into law, and Michael Bommarito counts 505 local data center moratoria adopted or pending in 42 states as of August 2026, 370 of them in force and 116 of those enacted in June 2026. New York's executive order of July 14, 2026, the only statewide measure, holds state permits for campuses of 50 megawatts or more. Since March 18, 2025, every new data center in Loudoun has needed a special exception, so each new campus goes before the supervisors with conditions attached. In Prince William, residents challenged the county's largest approval, the Digital Gateway rezonings of December 2023, and Virginia's Court of Appeals threw them out because the county's hearing notice didn't meet the statute. The zoning of the 37 planned buildings has reverted. A town with a moratorium gives up the property tax a campus would pay, $1.3 billion in Loudoun's fiscal 2027 budget, and it also gives up the chance to set terms like Loudoun's equipment rate or Chandler's noise baseline.

Richland Parish, Louisiana, where Meta is building its Hyperion campus, has been collecting sales tax on the construction itself. The sales tax on the site's construction materials, furniture and fixtures was cut to 1 percent. Even at that rate, the parish's first sales tax payment from the site came to $22.4 million, about half of it for the school board, The Advocate reported in June 2026. The board pays its staff a yearly bonus out of a one-cent sales tax dating from 1968, and that bonus went from $10,200 to $50,935 for certified staff and from $3,323 to $17,472 for classified staff. The superintendent, Sheldon Jones, expects the bonuses to stay high until construction ends, which is planned for 2030. House prices in the parish have risen the way Abilene's rents did. Redfin's median sale price, as reported by Moneywise, went from about $105,000 in November 2024 to about $295,000 in May 2026, though a parish of about 20,000 people records few sales in a month, so that median moves a lot from one month to the next.

11 · ARGUMENT

What the host decided

Quincy's rate fell under a levy cap that voters passed in 2001 and the legislature re-enacted in 2007. Washington's 2010 sales tax exemption applied only in rural counties like Grant, and the county's utility charges large new users at least the market price plus 5 percent, so their power doesn't raise other customers' bills. Loudoun taxes data center equipment at $4.15 per $100, while Henrico charged $0.40 for eight years. Texas connected 14 gigawatts in 2024 under a process that checks a plant for reliability only, while in PJM new plants waited in the queue as Virginia's legislature scheduled retirements. Abilene's council wrote nothing about housing into the Stargate campus's tax break, and rents rose before the new homes opened. Residents came out ahead where the rules that towns, counties and state legislatures had set let revenue or power supply grow with the campuses, and they paid more where new power plants and new housing came late.

The studies of household electricity costs end before the 2025 capacity charge, and the new large-load tariffs haven't been tested through a downturn. And Loudoun now depends heavily on one kind of taxpayer, whose equipment loses value every year and is being replaced less often, while no state has published an estimate of whether the sales tax exemption pays for itself.

PJM's next auction, for 2029/30, is the first test of whether the new connection cycle has added capacity, and a fourth straight result at the cap would mean it hasn't. The 529 apartments permitted in Abilene should be occupied in 2027, and Zillow's rent index for the area will record whether rents come down. Loudoun's supervisors will present their fiscal 2028 budget early in 2027, after leaving the real estate rate unchanged for 2026 for the first time in a decade. In that budget the supervisors will decide how much of the $1.3 billion to count on year after year.

SECOND-ORDER EFFECT · VALUING A NETWORK FROM ONE COUNTY

Newton County, Indiana, had two miles of a railroad branch line and no station. Its assessor could value only the track inside the county, which earned no income on its own, though the sixty-mile line from Templeton to Kankakee was worth much less without those two miles. Donaldson and Hornbeck estimate that without the railroads, American farmland in 1890 would have been worth little more than a third of what it was. Much of the network's value showed up in the price of farms, where no county's assessment of track could count it.

The Grange, a farmers' organization founded in 1867, had close to 800,000 members by the mid-1870s, and they organized against the railroads over freight and grain elevator rates. They paid those rates every harvest, while the rise in their land's value was spread across the network and hard to trace to any one railroad. Illinois capped railroad and elevator rates in 1871, and the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 required railroads to publish rates that were "reasonable and just." The railroads kept laying new track through those years of regulation. In 1976 Congress found that states were taxing railroads about 40 percent more than comparable commercial and industrial property, and the 4-R Act barred states from taxing railroad property at a higher rate than other businesses.

A county values a data center the way Newton County valued its two miles of track, by the building, the servers and the jobs inside the county line. What the servers compute is sold to businesses and households, most of them outside the county, and its value shows up in what those buyers produce. A person who uses AI can still oppose a campus in their own county, as a Grange farmer fought the freight rates of a railroad that had raised the value of his land. In both cases the person pays the cost directly, in rent, noise or a freight bill, while the gain is spread across the economy and can't be traced to one building or one line.

We expect the data center argument to follow the railroad argument from local objection to state and federal terms. FERC moved in that direction on June 18, 2026, when it ordered the regional grid operators it regulates to show that their rules for connecting loads over 50 megawatts are "just and reasonable," the standard the Interstate Commerce Act set for freight rates. Because a campus, like a railroad, can't move once it's built, we'd also expect a later fight over whether states may tax data centers more heavily than other businesses, the question Congress answered for railroads in 1976.
